title: 2 Kings 12:17–21
context: Hazael king of Syria captures Gath and turns toward Jerusalem. Jehoash sends him the dedicated treasures of earlier kings, his own dedicated gifts, and the gold of the temple and palace, and Hazael withdraws. Joash’s servants later conspire and kill him, and his son Amaziah reigns after him. Kings gives no reason for the conspiracy. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 24:17–25 adds that after Jehoiada’s death Joash and the leaders turned to idols, that Jehoiada’s son Zechariah was stoned in the temple court at the king’s command, and that Joash’s servants killed him because of it. Jesus speaks of the blood of a Zechariah killed between the sanctuary and the altar (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51). Many identify him with the Zechariah of 2 Chronicles 24, though Matthew calls him son of Barachiah, which has led others to suggest the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1) or another figure; the identification is debated. Both traditions read this section as narrative and see no doctrinal fork over the tribute or the assassination.

verses.text: Then Hazael king of Syria went up and fought against Gath, and took it; and Hazael set his face to go up to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then Hazael king of Syria attacks and captures Gath, and turns to go up against Jerusalem. A threat arises.

Arminian readers note that Hazael’s rise had been foretold by Elisha (8:12), and that the threat to Jerusalem tests how the king will respond.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Kings has already presented Hazael’s campaigns against the northern kingdom as the LORD cutting away parts of Israel (10:32), and that the parallel in 2 Chronicles 24:23–24 explicitly links the Syrian attack to Judah’s abandonment of the LORD after Jehoiada’s death.

Both traditions read the verse as narrative, noting that Kings itself gives no explicit reason for the attack here.

verses.text: Jehoash king of Judah took all the holy things that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah, his fathers, kings of Judah, had dedicated, and his own holy things, and all the gold that was found in the treasures of the LORD’s house, and of the king’s house, and sent it to Hazael king of Syria; and he went away from Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash takes all the dedicated things of earlier kings, his own dedicated gifts, and all the gold in the treasuries of the LORD’s house and the palace, and sends them to Hazael, who withdraws. The king pays tribute.

Arminian readers note that the king chooses to give away the treasures dedicated to God to secure safety, which sits uneasily with his earlier zeal for the temple.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the stripping of the temple treasures to buy off an enemy is a recurring and sorrowful motif in Kings (compare 1 Kings 15:18; 2 Kings 18:15–16), and that the narrator records it without comment.

Both traditions read the payment as narrative and do not build a doctrinal contrast on it.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Joash, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Joash’s acts and all he did are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. The narrator cites a source.

Arminian readers note that the reference to other records shows that the biblical narrator selected material for his purpose, and that readers should focus on what he chose to highlight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the book referred to is not the biblical book of Chronicles but an earlier royal record that has not survived, and that the inspired narrator drew on such sources under God’s guidance.

Both traditions read the notice as part of the standard closing formula for a king’s reign.

verses.text: His servants arose and made a conspiracy, and struck Joash at the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joash’s servants conspire and strike him down at the house of Millo, on the road down to Silla. His reign ends in violence.

Arminian readers note that Kings does not explain the motive, and the parallel in 2 Chronicles 24:25 attributes it to the blood of Jehoiada’s sons, after Joash turned to idols and had Zechariah stoned (24:17–22).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the location of Silla is unknown, and that the account in Chronicles adds the reason Kings does not give; many readers see the two accounts as complementary, each with its own emphasis.

Both traditions read the assassination as narrative and see no doctrinal fork over it.

verses.text: For Jozacar the son of Shimeath, and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, struck him, and he died; and they buried him with his fathers in David’s city; and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jozacar son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer, his servants, strike him, and he dies; he is buried with his fathers in David’s city, and Amaziah his son reigns. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 24:26 names the conspirators slightly differently.

Arminian readers note that Chronicles also says he was not buried in the tombs of the kings, a detail interpreters harmonize in different ways.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that despite Joash’s failures, David’s line continues through Amaziah, showing that God’s faithfulness to his promise did not depend on the faithfulness of each king; Jesus’ later words about Zechariah (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51) are often linked with this period, though the identification is debated.

Both traditions read the close of the reign as narrative.
